catalog_quote: Finally, stress in Nyiyaparli is typical for an Australian language. Primary stress almost always falls on the first syllable of a word, characterised by an increase in loudness. Secondary stress usually falls on every odd-numbered syllable. The last syllable that would receive secondary stress may optionally be unstressed. The examples in (2.3) illustrate this pattern. (2.3) a. ˈkantiˌpurrku ‘mob’ (Gordon Mackay in CvB02-000447B) b. ˈintinˌmalpi ‘rain-pst’ (David Stock in JB-20190621-02) c. ˈthungkuˌwayiˌlakaˌlay ‘cooked-inch-when’ (David Stock in JB-2019062-02) d. ˈnyupaˌngarniˌthakuru ‘spouse-prop-caus-sim=now’ (Gordon Mackay in CvB02-000447B)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable (impressionistic cue: loudness); secondary stresses on subsequent odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th..), i.e. left-to-right trochaic alternation; a final odd syllable may optionally go unstressed (no obligatory final secondary stress). Not weight-sensitive; not tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress usually falls on every odd-numbered syllable. The last syllable that would receive secondary stress may optionally be unstressed.' Examples mark secondary stress on syllables 3 (and 5, 7) of 4-, 5- and 7-syllable words, including across suffix/clitic boundaries (thungku-wayi-laka-lay, nyupa-ngarni-thakuru).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged 'almost always' for initial primary stress, no specific exceptions listed; optional non-stressing of a word-final odd syllable. Author notes phonology is treated only briefly as background to morphosyntax; stress description is impressionistic (no acoustic study of stress; the thesis's small acoustic study concerns vowels).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (grammatical/phonological) word including suffixes and enclitics, as the examples show secondary stress counted continuously across nominal suffixes, verbal inflections and the =lay clitic; examples drawn from connected narrative recordings (von Brandenstein 1960s tapes, Battin 2019 fieldwork), not citation forms specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: Battin 2019 describes Nyiyaparli as spoken by Nyiyaparli and Palyku people and treats Nyiyaparli and Palyku as varieties of one language ('Nyiyaparli/Palyku'), matching Glottolog's language-level node nija1241 'Nyiyaparli-Palyku' (ISO xny). Data come mainly from Gordon Mackay (von Brandenstein recordings, 1960s) and David Stock (2019); Battin notes some variation between speakers may be dialectal but does not assign the stress description to one dialect. The ANU repository records the work as an Honours thesis (Glottolog lists it as a masters thesis).

new_statements.quote: Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: initial syllable reading and with Battin 2019, but only as a generalisation over all WA languages south of the Kimberley; the work says nothing about Nyiyaparli stress specifically, so it should not be posted as a Nyiyaparli-specific source. download record: the listed open_url (coombs.anu.edu.au.. /WA/contents.htm) returned HTTP 404 (attempt 1); web.archive.org refused the connection by automated download (attempt 2). The 1996 web edition is the online version of the 1993 print edition (Pacific Linguistics C-124, CC-BY, doi:10.15144/PL-C124), which was already held by the project from the earlier stage and is the copy read here.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Blanket note in the handbook's pronunciation guide: in Western Australian Aboriginal languages generally, word stress usually falls on the first syllable. Not a Nyiyaparli-specific claim: the Nyiyaparli entry (4.5.6) is purely bibliographic, lists 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None' and contains no statement on stress or phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Thieberger's handbook follows von Brandenstein (1972c) in treating Nyiyaparli as a dialect of Palyku (with Nirrikudhu and Parndikurra), so its Nyiyaparli (4.5.6) and Palyku (4.5.7) entries cross-reference each other; neither entry has a grammar or a phonological sketch. The catalog's Nyiyaparli-specific stress evidence remains Battin 2019 (the honours thesis on Nyiyaparli itself).
